subject: biology-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Neural signalling
bigPicture: Neurons carry information as electrical impulses: sodium and potassium ions flowing through channels change the voltage across the membrane. At synapses, chemicals carry the signal across the gap. HL adds how action potentials work in detail, myelin, drugs that interfere, and summation.

keyIdeas.cue: What is the structure of a neuron?
keyIdeas.answer: A cell body (cytoplasm and nucleus) with nerve fibres: many short dendrites and usually one long axon. Impulses are conducted along these fibres. An example neuron is in the data booklet.

keyIdeas.cue: How is the resting potential generated?
keyIdeas.answer: The sodium–potassium pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. More positive charge leaves than enters, and some K⁺ leaks back out, so the inside is negative (about −70 mV): the membrane is polarised.
An action potential, a rapid reversal of membrane potential, that travels along the fibre. It is electrical because positive ions move.

Larger diameter conducts faster: squid giant axons are much faster than small unmyelinated fibres. Myelinated fibres are far faster than unmyelinated ones. Data on speed vs diameter can be analysed with correlation coefficients (r, and r² for how much variation is explained).
A junction between two neurons or between a neuron and an effector (e.g. muscle). In chemical synapses signals pass one way only, from presynaptic to postsynaptic.
An impulse depolarises the presynaptic membrane; calcium channels open and Ca²⁺ enters; Ca²⁺ acts as a signal causing vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter by exocytosis.

keyIdeas.cue: How is an excitatory postsynaptic potential generated?
keyIdeas.answer: Neurotransmitter (e.g. acetylcholine) diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptor proteins on the postsynaptic membrane, opening channels so Na⁺ enters and depolarises it. Acetylcholine works at many synapses, including neuromuscular junctions; acetylcholinesterase then breaks it down.

keyIdeas.cue: What happens during an action potential?
keyIdeas.answer: Stimulus brings the membrane to threshold (about −50 to −55 mV); voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ rushes in, depolarisation to about +30 mV. Then Na⁺ channels close and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, K⁺ leaves, repolarisation (briefly overshooting, hyperpolarisation). The pump restores the gradients.

keyIdeas.cue: How does an action potential propagate?
keyIdeas.answer: Na⁺ entering at one point diffuses along inside the axon (and positive charge outside moves the other way): these local currents bring the next region to threshold, so the impulse moves along. The region behind is refractory, so it moves one way.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you read an oscilloscope trace?
keyIdeas.answer: Flat line at −70 mV = resting potential; steep rise to +30 mV = depolarisation; fall = repolarisation; dip below −70 = hyperpolarisation; return to rest. Count peaks per second to find impulse frequency.
In myelinated fibres, ion channels and pumps are clustered at the gaps (nodes of Ranvier). The action potential jumps from node to node, so it is much faster.

keyIdeas.cue: How do neonicotinoids and cocaine affect synapses?
keyIdeas.answer: Neonicotinoids (insecticides) bind to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on insect postsynaptic membranes. Acetylcholinesterase cannot break them down, so the receptors stay occupied: normal signals can no longer get through, synaptic transmission is blocked and the insect is paralysed. They bind insect receptors far more strongly than mammalian ones. Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake, so dopamine stays in the cleft and keeps stimulating the postsynaptic neuron.

keyIdeas.cue: What does an inhibitory neurotransmitter do?
keyIdeas.answer: It opens channels (e.g. for Cl⁻ in, or K⁺ out) so the postsynaptic membrane becomes hyperpolarised (more negative), making an action potential less likely.
A postsynaptic neuron receives inputs from many presynaptic neurons. Excitatory and inhibitory potentials add up; only if the total reaches threshold does an action potential fire (all-or-nothing).

Free nerve endings in the skin have channels for positive ions that open in response to heat, acid or chemicals such as capsaicin. Cations enter, threshold is reached and impulses travel to the brain, where pain is perceived.
An emergent property arising from the interaction of huge numbers of neurons in the brain, not from any single neuron.

keyIdeas.cue: How fast are impulses, and what does an R² value tell you about speed data?
keyIdeas.answer: Roughly 1 m s⁻¹ in thin unmyelinated fibres, about 25 m s⁻¹ in the squid giant axon, and up to around 100 m s⁻¹ in myelinated fibres. R² (coefficient of determination) shows how much of the variation in speed is explained by, e.g., axon diameter: close to 1 means a tight fit.

keyIdeas.cue: Why is saltatory conduction also economical?
keyIdeas.answer: Ions only cross the membrane at the nodes, so fewer ions have to be pumped back by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump afterwards, saving ATP.

keyTerms.def: About −70 mV across a neuron's membrane when not conducting.
Rapid depolarisation and repolarisation that travels along a neuron.
Junction across which a neurotransmitter carries a signal.
Potential (about −50 to −55 mV) at which voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open.
Jumping of impulses between nodes of Ranvier.
Adding of postsynaptic potentials from many inputs.

workedExamples.title: Impulse frequency from a trace (AHL)
workedExamples.prompt: An oscilloscope trace shows 12 action potentials in 0.04 s. Calculate the frequency.
workedExamples.answer: 300 impulses per second. A stronger stimulus raises frequency, not peak size.

misconceptions.wrong: A stronger stimulus gives a bigger action potential.
misconceptions.right: Action potentials are all-or-nothing; stronger stimuli raise frequency.

misconceptions.wrong: Ions flow through the pump during an action potential.
misconceptions.right: Ions flow through voltage-gated channels; the pump restores gradients.

misconceptions.wrong: Myelin speeds impulses by conducting electricity.
misconceptions.right: It insulates, so impulses jump from node to node.

misconceptions.wrong: The refractory period is just the membrane recovering its charge.
misconceptions.right: Right after an action potential the Na⁺ channels are inactivated and cannot reopen, which is why impulses travel only one way.
